failures.en: Tag "DO NOT USE" (tag out defective equipment)
failures.reason: Internal register inconsistency: the embedded tag text "NO USAR" is an infinitive prohibition, but the glossary's binding register rule (usted imperative for instructions) is enforced on every parallel caps prohibition — the CRITICAL FAIL entry explicitly forbids "no operar (infinitive — instructions use usted imperative)", and NO ENTRE, EVACÚE, and the printed label ESCANEE ANTES DE OPERAR all use usted imperative. The app prints its own tags, and a defective unit will show tag "NO USAR" beside banner "FALLA CRÍTICA — NO OPERE" — two moods for the same command class, violating the one-register rule the glossary itself codifies.
failures.suggestion: etiquete "NO USE"

verdicts.lens: Register: usted, imperative, <=6th-grade reading level, no academic/legal jargon

failures.reason: The es value 'análisis de peligros del trabajo' deviates from the officially-used OSHA form. OSHA 3071's Spanish edition — which this entry's own note cites as its anchor — is titled 'Análisis de peligros en el trabajo', and the OSHA outreach/training ecosystem uniformly uses 'análisis de peligros en el trabajo (JHA)' (verified via web against osha.gov-linked course catalogs). DESIGN.md binds terminology to OSHA official Spanish where it exists, so the 'en el' form is the better-established term; 'del trabajo' is a near-synonym with no safety drift, but it breaks the official-anchor rule and would fail the glossary-consistency gate against OSHA-sourced copy.
failures.suggestion: análisis de peligros en el trabajo (JHA)

failures.reason: 'Chaqueta' has a divergent meaning across LatAm countries: in Mexico it is widely-known vulgar slang (the garment is 'chamarra' there), so the mandated term reads as crude to what is typically the largest Spanish-speaking nationality on US worksites, undermining the serious register of safety copy. The glossary bans milder cross-country collisions in the other direction ('cascos' for earmuffs, 'plática', 'pantalla facial'), so by its own standard this fails regional neutrality. Every single-country garment word (chamarra MX, campera AR, casaca PE) is equally regional, so the neutral fix is the garment-agnostic 'ropa protectora'.
failures.suggestion: EPP de soldadura (ropa protectora, guantes y careta)

failures.reason: Semantic drop: the es value back-translates as only 'hot work' — the '/ fire' half of the hazard label vanished. Every other slashed hazard row in this glossary translates all elements (silice/polvo/humos; resbalones, tropiezos y caidas; interaccion con publico y vehiculos), so a worker scanning the Spanish hazard list for a plain fire hazard (flammable storage, battery charging — the platform is safety-agnostic, not hot-work-only) finds no row covering it. Dropped condition = automatic FAIL under this lens.
failures.suggestion: trabajo en caliente / incendio

failures.reason: False-friend calque: 'anillo' in Spanish means only a ring-shaped object (jewelry/circle) and carries no acoustic sense, so 'prueba de anillo' back-translates as 'ring-object test' — the load-bearing meaning (tap the wheel and listen for a clear ring vs a dull thud BEFORE mounting) is unrecoverable from the term. Under stress a worker could look for a ring-shaped part or skip the check entirely and mount a cracked wheel (explosion hazard, 1910.215). The forbidden list ('prueba del aro') repeats the same calque instead of fixing it; the comprehensible 6th-grade term is the sound test.
failures.suggestion: prueba de sonido

failures.reason: Bare 'vigía' collides with the Fire watch entry: Attendant mandates es 'vigía' while the Fire watch entry's note says "UI standardizes 'vigía'" for that role too (its es is 'vigía de incendios'). Two distinct safety-critical roles share one head noun, and they co-occur on the same job whenever hot work happens in or near a confined space — both permit types exist in this app. A 'Vigía:' role field cannot tell workers which duty applies (the attendant must never leave the opening; the fire watch stays ≥30 min after hot work), so the ambiguity can leave an occupied confined space unattended. The glossary's own standard treats exactly this collision class as disqualifying (it forbids 'cascos' because it 'collides with hard hat' and 'equipo' because it 'collides with equipment'), so mandating the same bare term for two roles is internally inconsistent — and a safety-meaning ambiguity, which cannot pass.
failures.suggestion: vigía de espacio confinado (short form 'vigía' only inside unambiguous confined-space-only screens; correspondingly fix the Fire watch note to standardize the full 'vigía de incendios', never bare 'vigía')

failures.reason: Internal imperative-register contradiction: the note says the banner 'pairs with the NO USAR tag', but the glossary's own 'Tag DO NOT USE' entry mandates the tag text 'NO USE' and explicitly forbids 'NO USAR' as an infinitive that violates the caps usted-imperative rule (NO OPERE / NO ENTRE / NO USE). A translator following this note verbatim would print the banned infinitive on physical tags.
failures.suggestion: FUERA DE SERVICIO — with the note corrected to: "Caps on tags and banners; pairs with the 'NO USE' tag."

failures.reason: 'Engullimiento' is neither the OSHA-es nor the LatAm-regulatory term, and the note's claimed anchor is unsupported. Verified: OSHA's own Spanish grain-engulfment materials use 'atrapamientos/inmersiones'; OSHA-es confined-space definitions render engulf as 'envolver/sumergir a un entrante'; MX NOM-033-STPS-2015 says 'sumersión o inmersión'; Colombia Res. 0491/2020 says 'sepultar, sumergir, envolver o atrapar'. 'Engullir' is a food verb (gulp down) and its derived noun is rare, so crews may not recognize 'engullimiento' as this fatal confined-space/grain hazard — a comprehension gap on a life-critical hazard row.
failures.suggestion: atrapamiento e inmersión en material a granel (keep the existing plain gloss 'quedar sepultado por material a granel'; also correct the note's false OSHA-es attribution)

failures.reason: The es value 'FUERA DE SERVICIO' is correct, but the entry's note pairs it with "the 'NO USAR' tag" — the exact infinitive form the Tag "DO NOT USE" entry explicitly forbids (that entry mandates the usted-imperative tag text 'NO USE'). The glossary contradicts itself and, followed as written, would propagate the forbidden tag wording onto printed defective-equipment tags.
failures.suggestion: FUERA DE SERVICIO — unchanged; fix the note to read "pairs with the 'NO USE' tag" so it matches the mandated tag text

verdicts.lens: Regional neutrality (Iberian forms, country-specific slang, divergent meanings across LatAm)

failures.reason: Back-translation ambiguity on a life-safety alarm: bare 'ALTO' also means 'high', and this same glossary uses 'alto' as the risk level High ('nivel de riesgo: ... alto ...'). On an atmo-check screen next to elevated gas readings, 'ALTO' can be misread as a HIGH-reading label rather than a stop order — especially by South American workers, whose road-sign stop word is PARE (the note itself concedes this). A stressed worker parsing 'LEL 12% — ALTO' as 'LEL high' instead of 'STOP' is exactly the misread-under-stress failure this lens exists to catch.
failures.suggestion: DETENGA EL TRABAJO (always render the full usted imperative as the alarm state; if a short attention word is kept, only ever as 'ALTO — DETENGA EL TRABAJO', never bare 'ALTO' adjacent to gas readings or risk-level labels)

failures.reason: Semantic drift in the first half: 'firma de ingreso' back-translates as 'entry / sign-in signature'. In LatAm field Spanish 'ingreso' is the standard word for physically entering a site or confined space ('permiso de ingreso a espacio confinado'), so the phrase reads as an attendance/entry log — the roll-call meaning the entry itself forbids ('pase de lista') — and drops the safety meaning of sign-on: the crew signing that they have read and accept the plan's hazards and controls. On a job that also runs a confined-space permit, 'firma de ingreso (cuadrilla)' is plausibly misread as the entrant/entry record, a dangerous role confusion.
failures.suggestion: firma de aceptación del plan (cuadrilla) / firma de aprobación

failures.reason: Internal contradiction that mandates two conflicting prohibition tags: this entry's note says it 'pairs with the NO USAR tag', but the Tag "DO NOT USE" entry mandates the tag text 'NO USE' and explicitly forbids 'NO USAR' as an infinitive that breaks the usted-imperative rule for caps prohibitions (NO OPERE / NO ENTRE). Following this note verbatim prints defective-equipment tags in the exact forbidden form, so field tags will disagree ('NO USE' vs 'NO USAR') on the same prohibition.
failures.suggestion: FUERA DE SERVICIO (es value unchanged; correct the note to read: pairs with the 'NO USE' tag — matching the Tag "DO NOT USE" entry's mandated usted-imperative text)

failures.reason: Misquoted OSHA-es anchor: the note cites the heat campaign as 'Agua. Sombra. Descansos.' — the OSHA Heat Illness Prevention Campaign slogan is 'Water. Rest. Shade.', officially rendered 'Agua. Descanso. Sombra.' (singular, and Rest before Shade). The es value 'enfermedad por calor' is correct and industry-standard, but a verbatim-wrong anchor quote in the terminology ground-truth document fails anchor verification: translators copying the note's slogan onto worker-facing heat materials would print a corrupted version of the official campaign wording, and the glossary's authority rests on its anchors being checkable.
failures.suggestion: es stays 'enfermedad por calor'; correct the note's anchor quote to: OSHA-es heat campaign 'Agua. Descanso. Sombra.' uses 'enfermedades por calor'.

failures.en: Review status: Pending Review / Approved / Needs Revision / Recalled
failures.reason: Missed instance of the exact scoping-defect class round 2 fixed for 'sonido' and 'servicio': the forbidden terms 'rechazado (harsher than Needs Revision)' and 'devuelto' are unscoped, yet (a) the Approve/Deny entry mandates 'Rechazar' for the Deny button — the very action that produces this 'rejected' status (safety-types.ts:345 maps rejected→'Needs Revision'), (b) the worker-visible record timeline note renders 'Rejected: …' (safety-records.ts:776), and (c) HEAD banner copy reads 'record needs revision — returned by EHS' (en.json:125). A generator translating those real surfaces must either use a forbidden lexeme or invent unsanctioned phrasing, and a glossary-consistency scan flags the mandated 'Rechazar' against this entry's forbidden list.
failures.suggestion: es stays 'pendiente de revisión / aprobado / requiere correcciones / retirado'; scope the forbidden items per the round-2 convention: "rechazado (as the status label — the Deny action button 'Rechazar' is a different concept, see Approve/Deny entry; timeline note 'Rejected:' renders 'Rechazado:')" and "devuelto (as the bare status label; OK in prose such as 'devuelto por EHS para correcciones' when translating 'returned by EHS')".

failures.reason: Cross-entry contradiction on a single UI flow, verified against the app: the Deny action ('Rechazar') is what puts a record into the state the Review-status entry mandates as 'requiere correcciones' and explicitly forbids rendering as 'rechazado (harsher than Needs Revision)' (src/lib/safety-records.ts markReviewRejected → reviewStatus 'rejected'; src/lib/safety-types.ts:345 labels it 'Needs Revision'; src/app/safety/review/action/page.tsx confirms Deny → 'This record needs revision.'). So the worker presses 'Rechazar' and gets a status whose own glossary rationale says the rechaz- framing is too harsh — the two entries' notes disagree with each other, and the forbidden lexeme lacks the '(alone)/(as the status label)' scoping convention the round-2 fixes established for 'sonido' and 'servicio'. The trap is tightened by the same entry's unscoped forbidden 'devuelto' while the app's dashboard banner reads '… need revision — returned by EHS' (src/messages/en.json:125), leaving a translator no compliant rendering of 'returned'. Both prior rounds missed this because each entry passes in isolation.
failures.suggestion: Reconcile the pair explicitly. Either (a) keep 'Aprobar / Rechazar' and scope both sides: Review-status forbidden becomes "rechazado (as the status label — the Deny action button stays 'Rechazar'; the resulting status renders 'requiere correcciones')" plus a cross-reference in the Approve/Deny note ('Deny sets the record to requiere correcciones — see Review status'), and scope 'devuelto' for the dashboard banner ('returned by EHS' → 'devuelto por EHS' permitted in that banner only); or (b) align the action with the changes-requested semantics the product already uses ('returned by EHS'), e.g. 'Aprobar / Pedir correcciones', and keep 'rechazado' fully forbidden. Do not leave the mandate and the prohibition pointing at the same transition unscoped.

failures.reason: Stale/incorrect cross-reference between doNotTranslate and the entry note: doNotTranslate line 'Kept acronyms — expand in Spanish once, then keep: LOTO, JHA, PTP, SDS, EHS, …' orders a one-time Spanish expansion of EHS, but the EHS Review entry's note says 'EHS stays untranslated (brand acronym, doNotTranslate)' and supplies no expansion — while the brand line in doNotTranslate is 'Sage EHS (brand)', not bare EHS. Every other acronym in the expand-once list has a mandated Spanish expansion somewhere in the glossary (bloqueo y etiquetado/LOTO, análisis de peligros en el trabajo/JHA, plan previo a la tarea/PTP, hoja de datos de seguridad/SDS, límite inferior de explosividad/LEL, inmediatamente peligroso para la vida o la salud/IDLH, equipo de respiración autónoma/SCBA, plataforma de trabajo aéreo/MEWP, línea de vida autorretráctil/SRL, sistema personal de detención de caídas/PFAS, mantenimiento preventivo/PM, responsable directo del mantenimiento preventivo/DRI, Programa de Prevención de Lesiones y Enfermedades/IIPP); EHS alone has none. A translator following line 30 must invent an expansion the entry implicitly forbids; following the entry violates line 30.
failures.suggestion: Pick one policy and state it in both places: move EHS out of the expand-once list into the brand group (e.g. 'EHS (functional brand acronym — never expand, never substitute HSE/SSOMA)'), or mandate a single Spanish expansion in the entry (e.g. 'medio ambiente, salud y seguridad (EHS)' on first use) and keep it in the expand-once list. The entry note's citation of doNotTranslate must match what the list actually says.

No safety drift ('cumple / no cumple' is correct for item results), purely an internal forbidden-vs-mandated collision left behind by the corrections.

failures.en: registerRules[14] — safety-agnostic workplace vocabulary rule ('planta, bodega, taller, patio, sitio')
failures.reason: Country-divergent term embedded in the binding rules themselves, missed because prior regional-lens passes scanned only the 111 entries (round 2 verdict: passCount 111, entries only). 'Bodega' means warehouse in MX/CL/CO/Central America, but in Peru it is a neighborhood grocery store, in Argentina/Uruguay a winery (warehouse there = 'depósito'), in Cuba a ration store, and in US-Caribbean usage a corner store. The rule mandates this vocabulary for all workplace-general Spanish copy, so warehouse screens written per the rule will misread as 'store/winery' to Southern-Cone, Peruvian and Caribbean crews — the exact divergence class rules 8-9 ban and rule 18 ('one mandated term per concept; regional synonyms live only in notes') exists to prevent. No safety-meaning drift (location noun, not an instruction, hazard, or alarm), but it fails regional neutrality inside a binding rule and is mirrored uncorrected in the sign-off packet (docs/i18n/review/packet-glossary.md line 153).
failures.suggestion: In registerRules[14] replace 'bodega' with 'almacén' — the pan-regional professional logistics/warehousing register (WMS = 'gestión de almacenes' across all countries) and the term OSHA-es warehousing materials use — or the fully neutral 'área de almacenamiento'; if 'bodega' is kept at all, demote it to a note as a MX/CL/CO regional synonym per rule 18. Apply the same edit to the packet copy of the rule.

A forbidden-lexeme consistency gate, or a literal translator, flags the mandated Approved status as violating this entry.

failures.reason: The round-2 correction introduced a new same-screen collision and dropped a meaning half. (a) Collision: the corrected term 'atrapamiento e inmersión en material a granel' now leads with 'atrapamiento' — but the app's confined-space form renders 'Engulfment' and 'Configuration / entrapment' as adjacent chips in the SAME ChipMultiSelect (src/data/safety-checklists.ts:166, ConfinedSpaceForm.tsx:369), and CONFINED_SPACE_HAZARDS is translate-at-insertion data governed by this glossary (docs/i18n/DESIGN.md). 'Configuration / entrapment' has no glossary entry, and its natural OSHA-es rendering IS 'atrapamiento' (1910.146 configuration hazard: 'quedar atrapado por paredes convergentes'). Two distinct fatal confined-space hazards now share one head noun in one multiselect — the exact collision class the glossary itself treats as disqualifying (vigía, cascos, equipo). (b) Dropped half: 1910.146 engulfment covers capture by 'a liquid or finely divided (flowable) solid'; 'material a granel' back-translates as bulk (granular) material only, and the forbidden 'ahogamiento (drowning — different)' further steers translators away from the liquid reading — so water/sewage/sludge inflow, a dominant confined-space killer, loses its hazard chip meaning.
failures.suggestion: Re-term engulfment without the colliding head noun and with the liquid half restored — e.g. 'inmersión o sepultamiento en líquidos o material a granel' (plain gloss 'quedar sepultado o sumergido') — and ADD a 'Configuration / entrapment' entry that owns 'atrapamiento' (e.g. 'atrapamiento por la forma interna del espacio (paredes convergentes)'), with mutual cross-notes so the two chips can never render with the same head word.
failures.lens: Safety accuracy (final adversarial verification): back-translation for semantic drift, dropped meaning halves, stress-misreadable ambiguity in alarm states / prohibition tags / atmospheric terms, plus hunt for collisions and stale cross-references introduced or missed by the two prior fix rounds

A translator following the note verbatim prints bare 'eslinga' in fall-protection UI.
